statement: In one laboratory trial of 17 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (398 days on average), each of whom completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart, cannabis flower inhaled from a desktop vaporizer, compared with the same flower smoked in a small handheld pipe (10 mg or 25 mg of THC loaded, from 13.4% THC flower, taken over 10 minutes; study conditions only), was associated with higher average peak ratings of drug effect on a 0 to 100 scale at the lower amount (69.5 against 45.7; editors' calculation of the difference, 23.8 points, 95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) but with no flagged difference at the higher amount (77.5 against 66.4), and with a larger rise in heart rate at the lower amount (23.3 against 11.3 beats a minute) but not at the higher. Average peak whole-blood THC was also higher after vaporizing (7.5 against 3.8 ng/mL, and 14.4 against 10.2), but the paper reports no test of that difference and the editors' intervals for it include zero. On attention and psychomotor tasks, three contrasts between the methods were flagged, all showing worse performance after vaporizing; at the higher amount both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects, anxiety, memory impairment and throat irritation or coughing over placebo, with no flagged difference between them. Three adverse events were reported, all at the higher amount (vomiting once after each method, hallucinations once after vaporizing), too few to compare. Effects outlasted blood THC, which was back to zero within 4 hours while drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours. Only some contrasts between the methods were flagged, and none was corrected for the 32 outcomes. The authors say that earlier comparisons (not read here) found similar profiles for the two methods, and suggest that those let people adjust their own dose. This trial gave a fixed amount of one flower to people who rarely use cannabis, with one pipe and one vaporizer, in a laboratory, and followed people only through each session. The authors note that the largest amount given was smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (from a survey they cite, not read here). It did not test joints, bongs, portable vaporizers, oil cartridges, concentrates, tobacco mixed in, self-paced or repeated use, or effects on the lungs, and it did not measure how much THC left each device. Funding as printed: a US federal health agency (SAMHSA), which also provided technical assistance on design, analysis, interpretation and manuscript approval; one author reports consulting fees or honoraria from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Insys Therapeutics, Battelle Memorial Institute and Canopy Health Innovations; no industry funding is printed.
plain: In one small laboratory study, 17 healthy adults who rarely use cannabis took the same cannabis flower two ways on different days, smoked in a small pipe and breathed in from a vaporizer, and also had a dummy version of each. At the lower of two amounts, vaporizing gave higher scores for how strong the effect felt, and a bigger rise in heart rate, than smoking; at the higher amount the two ways did not clearly differ. Average blood THC was higher after vaporizing, but the study did not test whether that was more than chance. Both ways made some tasks harder, and three bad reactions were reported (vomiting twice, hallucinations once), too few to compare the two ways. This was one small study in a laboratory with fixed amounts, one pipe and one vaporizer. It did not test joints, vape pens, oil cartridges or concentrates, and says nothing about the lungs or regular use.
population: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days since last use, median 365 days)
exposure: Cannabis flower (13.4% THC) vaporized in a desktop vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, with 10 mg or 25 mg of THC in the material loaded, over 10 minutes (study conditions only)
comparator: The same flower with the same THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe in the same people; each method also had a placebo session (flower under 0.01% THC) as its reference
outcome: Peak ratings of drug effect and other effects, heart rate and blood pressure, whole-blood THC, performance on attention and psychomotor tasks, and adverse events, within 8.5-hour sessions
magnitude: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo 11.2 and 2.1. Vaporized minus smoked, editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg; 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg. Heart rate rise, beats per minute, mean (SD): smoked 11.3 (10.4) and 19.1 (17.1); vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); only the 10 mg difference between methods flagged; editors' unpaired differences 12.0 (4.2 to 19.8) and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5). Peak whole-blood THC, ng/mL, mean (SD): smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4); vaporized 7.5 (5.5) and 14.4 (9.4); no test reported; editors' unpaired differences 3.7 (-0.3 to 7.7) and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9). Differences between methods flagged: 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg; 3 task contrasts (Divided Attention distance at 10 mg; Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg); none corrected across 32 outcomes. Adverse events: 3 reported among 17 people, all in 25 mg sessions. Blood THC back to zero within 4 hours; drug-effect ratings above baseline at 6 hours after both 25 mg conditions.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Methods › Study Design and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27.3) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days, median 365, range 30 to 1,825 since last use) each completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart: flower with 0, 10 or 25 mg THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe or vaporized in a Volcano Medic vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, over 10 minutes. Method order was counterbalanced across people and dose order randomized within each method.

Flower from the US National Institute on Drug Abuse supply with 13.4% delta-9-THC (placebo batch under 0.01%); the same weight of plant material (186.6 mg) in every session, with placebo material mixed in to reach 10 mg. The 'dose' is the THC in the material loaded; the paper does not report how much THC left each device.

evidence.locator: Table (Drug effect row); Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract
evidence.extracted: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak change: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo (0 mg) sessions 11.2 (15.9) smoked and 2.1 (5.2) vaporized. Vaporized exceeded smoked at 10 mg (flagged P below .05) and no difference was flagged at 25 mg. Editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): vaporized minus smoked 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg and 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg.

evidence.locator: Results › Whole-Blood THC Concentrations, 1st paragraph; Abstract
evidence.extracted: Peak whole-blood THC, mean (SD) ng/mL: vaporized 7.5 (5.5) at 10 mg and 14.4 (9.4) at 25 mg; smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4). Peak at the first sample (10 minutes), back to zero within 4 hours in every condition. The paper reports no test or interval for the difference between methods. Editors' calculation (unpaired): vaporized minus smoked 3.7 ng/mL (-0.3 to 7.7) at 10 mg and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9) at 25 mg.

evidence.locator: Table (Physiological measures); Results › Physiological Measures, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Heart rate, mean (SD) peak rise in beats per minute: smoked 11.3 (10.4) at 10 mg and 19.1 (17.1) at 25 mg; vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); placebo (0 mg) sessions -3.7 smoked and -4.3 vaporized. Only the 10 mg difference between methods was flagged (P below .05); editors' calculation (unpaired), vaporized minus smoked: 12.0 beats per minute (4.2 to 19.8) at 10 mg and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5) at 25 mg. Peak at the first measurement (10 minutes); back to baseline within 3 hours.

evidence.locator: Table (Cognitive measures); Results › Cognitive and Psychomotor Measures, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Task performance, peak change from baseline. Digit Symbol Substitution (number correct): vaporized -8.3 at 10 mg and -13.8 at 25 mg, both below the vaporized placebo session; smoked +3.4 and -7.0, neither different from its placebo session. Differences between methods at the 10 and 25 mg doses were flagged for three contrasts only: Divided Attention distance at 10 mg, and Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg (the Table also carries the between-method flag on two 0 mg vaporized cells, Divided Attention distance and Divided Attention total correct). Deficits typically peaked 30 to 60 minutes after dosing and in some instances had not returned to baseline at 6 to 8 hours.

evidence.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table
evidence.extracted: At 25 mg both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects (smoked 32.9, vaporized 24.4), anxious or nervous (21.4; 25.5), memory impairment (14.2; 16.2), throat irritation or coughing (27.8; 22.18) and difficulty performing routine tasks (30.6; 34.2) over placebo, with no difference between methods flagged for the unpleasant, anxious, memory or throat items. Paranoid ratings rose over placebo only after vaporized 25 mg; sick only after smoked 25 mg. Between-method differences were flagged for 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg.

Adverse events as reported: two people vomited (one after 25 mg vaporized, one after 25 mg smoked) and one had hallucinations after 25 mg vaporized. No counts are given for placebo or 10 mg sessions and no other events are listed; the paper gives no incidence figures behind the abstract's statement of increased incidence of adverse effects at 25 mg, and these three are the only events it lists.

evidence.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 2nd paragraph; Results › Correlations Between Whole-Blood THC Concentrations and Pharmacodynamic Profiles; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: After both 25 mg conditions mean drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours (smoked 12.2, vaporized 10.8) although blood THC was back to zero within 4 hours. Blood THC correlated with drug-effect ratings (r above 0.37) and heart rate (r above 0.24) but, for performance, only with Digit Symbol Substitution correct at 25 mg vaporized (r = -0.32); the authors conclude that blood THC is not a valid indicator of intoxication or impairment.

The authors state that earlier controlled comparisons (not read here) found similar profiles for smoked and vaporized cannabis, and suggest that the different result here may be because those studies let people adjust their dose while this one gave a fixed amount, and that vaporizing delivers THC more efficiently because smoking loses THC to combustion and side-stream smoke (not tested).

Limits stated by the authors: a limited range of doses, one type of cannabis (raw plant material, high THC, low cannabidiol), one vaporizer at a fixed temperature, enrolment limited to people who rarely use cannabis, and a sample too small to study individual characteristics. They note that the largest amount given (0.19 g of 13.4% THC flower) is smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (about 1 g, often over 18% THC, citing a 2018 paper that was not read here).

evidence.locator: Study Registration Dates; Study Overview; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures; Design Details
evidence.extracted: Registry record NCT03676166: study start 16 June 2016, completion 17 January 2017, first submitted 16 September 2018 (after the study ended); actual enrolment 18 against 17 analysed in the paper; registered primary outcome quantity of THC in blood at 8 hours; secondary outcomes drug-effect rating, Digit Symbol Substitution, Paced Auditory Serial Addition and Divided Attention.

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis; Methods › Study Design and Procedure, 1st paragraph; Table (all rows)
evidence.extracted: The Table reports 32 outcomes (editors' count). Contrasts against placebo within each method used a threshold of P below .025 (Bonferroni for two comparisons); the contrasts between methods at each amount were treated as orthogonal and tested at P below .05 with no correction; nothing was corrected across the 32 outcomes (up to 192 planned contrasts, editors' count), and no interval or exact P value is given for any contrast. No double-dummy procedure was used to hide the inhalation method from participants and staff. The sample size of 17 was justified by a meta-analysis of six acute drug administration studies (reference 24), not by a cannabis route comparison.

evidence.locator: Article notes (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor)
evidence.extracted: Funding as printed: the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA, a US federal agency), which also provided technical assistance on design and conduct, analysis and interpretation, and preparation, review and approval of the manuscript and the decision to submit it; it had no role in collecting or managing study data. Disclosures as printed: Dr Vandrey reports personal fees, consulting or honoraria from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Insys Therapeutics, Battelle Memorial Institute and Canopy Health Innovations Inc outside the submitted work; Drs Vandrey, Spindle and Mitchell report SAMHSA grants during the study; Dr Cone reports consulting for ConeChem Research and RTI during the study; Dr Schlienz reports National Institute on Drug Abuse grants outside the work; Dr Hayes reports funding from the Department of Health and Human Services, SAMHSA, the National Laboratory Certification Program and RTI International.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 'some concerns' overall: sequence generation not described; the person inhaling knows the method and the main ratings are self-reported; registered after the study ended, with 32 outcomes and no correction for multiple comparisons; one implausible blood-pressure value and some text-versus-table mismatches.

inconsistency.note: One trial. Earlier smaller comparisons the authors cite reportedly found similar profiles for the two methods; they were not read.

indirectness.note: Worded for this trial's people and conditions. Read as a claim about vaping against smoking as people do them (joints, bongs, portable pens, cartridges, regular use, self-paced), it would be indirect.

imprecision.note: 17 people; wide interval for the lower-amount difference in drug-effect ratings; higher-amount difference includes zero; blood THC difference untested; between-method differences flagged for only a few items.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory trial with counterbalanced method order and randomized dose order starts high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias -1: RoB 2 'some concerns' in four of six domains (sequence generation not described; method cannot be hidden and the main ratings are self-reported; late registration with 32 uncorrected outcomes). Imprecision -1: 17 people; the lower-amount difference in drug-effect ratings has a wide interval (5.4 to 42.2), the higher-amount difference includes zero, the blood THC difference was not tested, and between-method differences were flagged for only 4 of 20 rating items at the lower amount, 2 at the higher and 3 task contrasts. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for this trial's people and conditions; strict reading: as a claim about vaping against smoking in everyday use it would be indirect and the certainty would be very low. Not downgraded for inconsistency or publication bias on one trial; the earlier comparisons the authors cite, which they say found similar profiles, were not read and would matter if they had been. Worded as an association rather than 'increases' because only some contrasts were flagged, none was corrected for the number of outcomes, and the trial is small.

verification.flag_note: Section 7 draft for the senior author (decision p-ways-of-taking); findings only, no advice. Rests on one 17-person crossover trial (Spindle 2018). The earlier smoked-against-vaporized comparisons the authors cite were not read, so the claim is shown as a single study although its authors say earlier studies found similar profiles; those would be the independent work to pair with it. Trial amounts appear only as study conditions. No industry funding is printed; one author's consulting ties are reported as printed. No awaited PDF is needed for this claim.
